subject: b95J01:B1-B4 — why package the exponents as the subgroup T of Z

nodes.claim: Why look at the set T = {m : g^m in H} instead of arguing with a minimal k and the division algorithm directly?

It is the same argument, packaged: T is the preimage of H under m ↦ g^m, a subgroup of Z, so one cyclic-generator statement delivers the least positive element and the divisibility for all integers m, negative ones included, at once.
Arguing directly needs a least positive exponent by well-ordering, then a division algorithm run to show every other exponent is a multiple of it, with negative exponents handled separately.
Replace both bookkeeping steps by the single statement that T = {m : g^m in H} is a subgroup of Z.
T is preserved under differences because m ↦ g^m is a homomorphism Z → G and H is closed under products and inverses.
Membership in T is literally membership of g^m in H, so facts about T translate into facts about powers landing in H with no extra work.
Use that every subgroup of Z is generated by one integer a, and that a is nonzero once T contains a positive integer.
With k = |a|, the equivalence g^m in H iff k divides m holds for every integer m, positive or negative.
Minimality and divisibility, the two conclusions of part (a), both fall out of the one subgroup statement.
